takeaway: Anal squamous-cell cancer is usually an HPV-related cancer treated with chemoradiation; persistent or recurrent disease goes to salvage surgery, and metastatic disease to systemic therapy [1].
clinicalQuestion: How is anal canal squamous-cell cancer treated by stage?
background: Anal cancer is uncommon but increasing, and squamous-cell carcinoma is the dominant histology [1].
intervention: Chemoradiation for early-stage disease; systemic therapy for metastases; salvage surgery after failure.
mainFindings: Anal cancer is about 2% of gastrointestinal malignancies. Incidence of all stages of anal squamous-cell cancer has been increasing, by 2.7% annually in the last decade in the review's citation. HPV is a key risk factor in 80–85% of cases, mostly HPV-16. Chemoradiation remains the mainstay for most patients with early-stage disease. Systemic therapy is the primary treatment for metastatic disease. Persistent disease or recurrence after chemoradiation is treated with salvage surgery [1].
clinicalMeaning: Do not send localised anal squamous-cell cancer straight to abdominoperineal resection; chemoradiation is the mainstay, with surgery reserved for failure [1].
limitations: This is a review, so it does not replace a guideline dose schedule. Drug doses are not used here because this summary stays with the review's stage framework [1].
bottomLine: HPV-related squamous-cell cancer of the anus is treated first with chemoradiation when localised, with salvage surgery if that fails [1].
practiceImplication: Ask about immunosuppression and HPV, and do not omit surveillance, because salvage surgery can still be curative for persistence [1].
trustRationale: Recent open review of the whole pathway; not a graded guideline.
whatNotToOverclaim: Do not invent mitomycin doses from this summary.
